units.title: Hello, Delphi!
units.summary: Write your first Delphi console program and print text and numbers with Write and Writeln.

lesson.md: Delphi is a tool for writing programs in the language **Object Pascal**. A Delphi program starts with the word `program` and a name. Its main part is a block between `begin` and `end.`, and the computer runs the lines in this block from top to bottom.

Line by line: `program Hello;` gives the program a name. `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` is a **compiler directive**: it tells Delphi to build a console program, which writes text into a terminal window. `Writeln` writes the text inside the parentheses `( )` and then ends the line. The program ends with `end` and a period `.`.

Each instruction is a **statement**. A semicolon `;` separates two statements. Text goes in single quotes, like `'Hi'`. Delphi does not care about upper or lower case in names: `Writeln`, `WriteLn` and `WRITELN` are the same.

`Write` writes without ending the line. If you give `Writeln` several values, separated by commas, it writes them one after the other with no space between them. `Writeln` without values writes an empty line. Numbers have no quotes, so Delphi can calculate with them: `+` adds and `*` multiplies.
To put a single quote inside a text, write it twice. `'It''s'` is the text `It's`. Inside quotes, `2 + 3` is only text, so Delphi does not calculate it.
Text between `{` and `}` or after `//` is a **comment**, and Delphi ignores it. `{$` is special: `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` is not a comment but an instruction for the compiler.
The last `end` of the program needs a period, not a semicolon. Text uses single quotes `'`, never double quotes `"`.

card: `program Name;` + `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` start a console program
`Writeln('Hi')` writes a line, `Write` stays on the line

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables with var and const, and meet Integer, Double, string, Boolean and Char.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Delphi you declare every variable before `begin`, in a `var` section. You write the name, a colon `:` and the **type**. The type says what kind of value the variable can hold.

lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
Next year: 37

lesson.md: `:=` is the **assignment** operator: it stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. `Age := Age + 1` reads the old value, adds 1 and stores the result. A single `=` compares two values; it does not assign.

`Integer` holds whole numbers and `Double` holds numbers with a decimal point. `string` holds text, `Boolean` holds `True` or `False`, and `Char` holds exactly one character, written in single quotes like `'A'`. You can declare several variables of the same type in one line: `A, B: Integer`.

`Writeln(Price:0:2)` writes a `Double` with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point. The first number is the minimum width, and `0` means as wide as needed. Without this format, Delphi writes a `Double` in a long scientific notation with an `E`.
`/` always gives a `Double`, even for two whole numbers. For whole-number division, use `div`. `mod` gives the remainder of that division.

A **constant** never changes. Declare it in a `const` section with `=` instead of `:=`. Delphi takes the type from the value. If you try to assign a new value to a constant, the program does not compile.

Delphi is **strongly typed**: every variable keeps its type. You cannot store a text in an `Integer` variable, and `Count := 2.5` does not compile when `Count` is an `Integer`. Names are not case sensitive: `age` and `Age` are the same variable.

card: `var Age: Integer;` declares a variable before `begin`
`div` and `mod` for whole numbers, `/` gives a `Double`

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Join text with +, measure it with Length, and search, cut and change it with Pos, Copy, UpperCase and Format.

lesson.md: A `string` holds a text of any length. The `+` operator joins two strings into a new one. This is called **concatenation**.
`Length(S)` returns the number of characters in `S`. Square brackets read one character: `S[1]` is the first character, because Delphi strings start counting at 1. One character has the type `Char`.

The unit `SysUtils` contains many helpers. To use it, add `uses SysUtils;` after `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}`. `UpperCase` and `LowerCase` change the case of the letters, and `Trim` removes spaces at both ends. `IntToStr` turns a number into a string, so you can join it with `+`.

`Pos(Sub, S)` returns the position where `Sub` first appears in `S`, or `0` if it is not there. `Copy(S, Start, Count)` returns `Count` characters of `S`, starting at position `Start`. If `Count` goes past the end, `Copy` stops at the last character.
`Format` from `SysUtils` builds a string from a pattern and a list of values in square brackets. Each placeholder is replaced by the next value: `%s` for a string and `%d` for an integer.
`+` only joins strings. `'Age: ' + 36` does not compile; write `'Age: ' + IntToStr(36)` instead. Inside `Writeln` you can also use commas: `Writeln('Age: ', 36)`.

exercises.explain: `Length` counts every character, and the space counts too: 5 + 1 + 5 = 11.

exercises.explain: Position 4 is the `b`. From there, `Copy` takes 5 characters: `board`.

exercises.explain: `Pos` returns the first position. In `banana`, the first `a` is the second character.

exercises.explain: Delphi strings start counting at 1, so the first character is `S[1]`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, then and else, combine conditions with and, or and not, and pick a branch with case.

lesson.md: A program can make decisions. `if Condition then Statement` runs the statement only when the condition is `True`. A condition is a `Boolean` expression, for example a comparison.
The comparison operators are `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Remember: Delphi uses a single `=` to compare and `:=` to assign.
`else` gives a second path for the case that the condition is `False`. If a path needs more than one statement, put the statements in a `begin ... end` block.

To test several conditions one after the other, write `else if`: `if Score >= 90 then ... else if Score >= 70 then ... else ...`. Delphi checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is `True`.
Never put a semicolon before `else`. The semicolon ends the whole `if` statement, so the `else` that follows has no `if`, and the program does not compile.

`and` is `True` when both sides are `True`. `or` is `True` when at least one side is `True`, and `not` turns `True` into `False` and back. Put each comparison in parentheses, like `(Age >= 13) and (Age <= 19)`. Without them, Delphi reads `and` first and the code does not compile.

`case` picks one branch by the value of an **ordinal** expression, which is a type with countable values, such as `Integer` or `Char`. Each branch has one or more values or a range like `1..5`, then a colon. `else` catches all other values. `case` does not work with strings.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for to and downto, while and repeat until, and visit every element of an array with for in.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop counts: `for I := 1 to 3 do` runs its statement with `I` set to 1, 2 and 3. The counter is a variable that you declare yourself, usually an `Integer`. With `downto`, the loop counts backwards.
If the start value is already past the end value, the body does not run at all. When the body has more than one statement, put them in a `begin ... end` block.
`while Condition do` checks the condition **before** each round and repeats while it is `True`. Make sure that the body changes something in the condition, or the loop never ends.

`repeat ... until Condition` checks the condition **after** each round, so the body always runs at least once. The loop stops as soon as the condition is `True`. It needs no `begin ... end`, even for several statements.

An **array** is a list of values of the same type. `Names: array of string` declares one, and `Names := ['Ada', 'Bob', 'Cy']` fills it. `for Name in Names do` visits every element, one after another, without a counter. The unit about arrays shows more.

lesson.output:
Hello, Ada
Hello, Bob
Hello, Cy

lesson.md: `Break` leaves a loop at once, and `Continue` jumps to the next round.
Do not change the counter of a `for` loop inside the loop; Delphi does not allow it. After the loop, the value of the counter is undefined, so do not use it there.

units.title: Procedures and functions
units.summary: Group code into procedures and functions, return values with Result, and pass parameters by value, var, const and out.

lesson.md: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you like. You declare it above the main `begin` of the program. To run it, write its name. This is a **call**.

**Parameters** pass values into a routine. You list them in parentheses, each with its type. A **function** also returns a value: its type comes after the colon, and you set the value by assigning it to `Result`.
A routine can have its own `var` section, like `I` in `Greet`. These **local variables** exist only while the routine runs, and only the routine can see them.

A normal parameter is a copy: changes inside the routine do not change the variable of the caller. A `var` parameter is the caller's variable itself, so the routine can change it. A `const` parameter cannot be changed inside the routine; use it for strings, because it avoids a copy.
An `out` parameter is like `var`, but it only passes a value **out** of the routine, so the routine must set it. Use `out` when a routine gives back more than one value.
Two routines can have the same name if their parameters differ. Mark each of them with the directive `overload`. Delphi then picks the one that fits the arguments of the call.
A routine must be declared before you call it. Put procedures and functions above the main `begin` of the program, and above other routines that call them.

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Store many values in static and dynamic arrays, size them with SetLength, and loop over them with Length, Low and High.

lesson.md: An **array** holds many values of the same type under one name. A **static array** has a fixed size that is part of its type: `array[1..3] of Integer` has three elements with the indexes 1, 2 and 3. You read and write an element with its index in square brackets.

`Low(A)` returns the first index of the array `A`, `High(A)` returns the last index, and `Length(A)` returns the number of elements. Use `Low` and `High` in `for` loops, so that the loop still works when the size changes.
The indexes of a static array can start at any number, for example at 0. A constant array lists its values in parentheses: `const Days: array[0..2] of string = ('Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed');`.

A **dynamic array** has no size in its type: `array of Integer`. `SetLength(A, 3)` gives it 3 elements, and a later `SetLength` can make it bigger or smaller while it keeps the existing values. A dynamic array always starts at index 0, so the last index is `Length(A) - 1`, which is the same as `High(A)`.
You can also fill a dynamic array in one step with square brackets: `Names := ['Ada', 'Bob']`. To add one element, make the array one element longer and store the value at the new last index.
A parameter like `const Values: array of Integer` is an **open array**. It accepts a static array, a dynamic array or a list in square brackets. Inside the routine, it always starts at index 0.

Never use an index outside the array. A dynamic array with 3 elements has the indexes 0, 1 and 2, so `A[3]` does not exist. Reading or writing there is a serious bug: the program may crash or use wrong data.

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Define your own types with classes: fields, a constructor, methods and properties, and free objects when you are done.

lesson.md: A **class** is a blueprint for objects. It bundles data, the **fields**, with the routines that work on this data, the **methods**. A method can be a procedure or a function. You declare a class in a `type` section, and by convention class names start with `T`.

`TPerson.Create` creates a new object, an **instance** of the class, and the variable `P` refers to it. A dot gives you access to its fields and methods: `P.Name`, `P.Greet`. You write the body of a method below the class, with the class name in front: `procedure TPerson.Greet;`. Inside the method, the fields can be used directly by name.

Delphi does not clean up objects for you. When you no longer need an object, call its method `Free`. Use `try ... finally`: the code after `finally` runs even when an error happens in the `try` part, so the object is always freed.

A **constructor** sets up a new object. Declare it with `constructor Create(...)` and give it parameters for the starting values. Its first statement `inherited Create;` runs the basic setup that every object needs.

Fields in a `private` section are meant only for the class itself; code in other units cannot see them. By convention, their names start with `F`. A **property** gives controlled access: `read` names where the value comes from, and `write` names where a new value goes. A property without `write` is read-only.

`Balance` has only `read`, so `Acc.Balance := 100` does not compile. The only way to change the balance is `Deposit`, which ignores amounts that are not positive. This keeps the object in a valid state.
A variable of a class type only refers to an object. Before `Create`, it refers to no object, and using it crashes the program. After `Free`, do not use the object again.

card: `type TPerson = class ... end;` declares a class
`property Age: Integer read FAge write FAge;`
`try ... finally P.Free; end;` frees the object
